whyThisMatters: A lot of what feels true about security is old advice or only partly right. A few minutes here will clear up what really matters.
rememberThis: If a security rule sounds old, check it again before you follow it.

discussionPrompts: Ask if anyone has seen a phishing email that looked correct and professional, with no spelling mistakes. What helped them notice it was fake?
For the password questions, ask if anyone still changes their password every 30 to 90 days just because they always did. Ask where that habit came from.
For the reporting questions, ask the group honestly: would you report something you were not sure was harmful? What would make it easier to report?
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People most often get mf-04 wrong. "P@ssw0rd!" looks strong because a letter is swapped for a symbol. So many people say TRUE. But it is actually false. Attackers already expect this trick.

items.myth: You can always tell a phishing email because of bad spelling and grammar.
items.fact: Modern phishing emails often look clean and professional. Many are written or fixed with AI tools. So spelling mistakes are not a reliable warning sign.
items.detail: The real clue is usually the sender's exact address, a request you did not expect, or pressure to act fast. It is not typos.

items.myth: If an email comes from someone I know, it's safe.
items.fact: Attackers often fake or take over real accounts, including coworkers' accounts. A familiar name does not prove a message is real.
items.detail: If a request feels strange, check using a different method, like a phone call, before you act on it.

items.fact: Phishing can now happen by text, phone call, QR code, or chat app like Teams. Any way to send a link or request can be used for an attack.
items.detail: The pattern is always the same. It uses urgency, a request, and pressure to act now. The channel does not matter.

items.myth: A password with a special character like "P@ssw0rd!" is strong.
items.fact: Length matters more than complexity. A longer plain phrase is harder to guess than a short password with symbol swaps that attackers already expect.
items.detail: "P@ssw0rd!" can be guessed in less than a second. A random 16-character phrase can take hundreds of years.

items.myth: You should change your password every 30-90 days.
items.fact: Forcing you to change passwords often usually leads to weaker, easier-to-guess passwords. A strong, unique password is fine to keep. Change it only if you have a real reason to think it was leaked.
items.detail: Most current advice no longer says to change passwords on a schedule. It focuses on three things: make it long, use a different password for each account, and watch for leaks.

items.myth: Reusing one strong password across a few accounts is fine, since it's strong.
items.fact: If one of those accounts is leaked, the same password will open every other account that uses it. A strong password does not protect you if you reuse it.
items.detail: A password manager helps you use a different password for each account. You do not need to remember them all.

items.fact: It is the planned use of urgency, authority, and trust to make you skip your normal checks. The pressure is the point, not just the lie.
items.detail: Attackers study how people act under pressure. Then they write a message to cause that reaction.

items.myth: Only careless or untrained people fall for social engineering.
items.fact: Well-designed social engineering can trick careful people too. It targets normal human reactions to urgency and authority. It does not only work on people who lack training.
items.detail: The goal of training is not to make you doubt everything. It is to help you pause before you act when you feel pressure.

items.myth: Reporting a mistake will get you in trouble.
items.fact: Reporting quickly is what protects you and the company. The damage usually comes from waiting, not from the first click.
items.detail: Security teams would rather check ten false alarms than learn about one real attack a week too late.

items.myth: If I am not sure something is harmful, it is not worth reporting.
items.fact: Security teams would rather check a false alarm than miss a real attack. If you are unsure, that is exactly when you should report.
items.detail: A five-minute report takes far less time than the hours needed to fix an attack found too late.
